rest.ups-module-redundancy: Redundancy topology and manufacturer part-load curves govern.
rest.ujoint-operating-angle: A single joint at angle b swings the output speed between cos(b) and 1/cos(b) of input TWICE per rev -- a peak-to-peak variation of 1/cos(b) - cos(b): 3.1% at 10 deg, 0.3% at 3 deg, 6.9% at 15 deg. A two-joint driveshaft CANCELS it only when BOTH working angles are equal AND the yokes are phased in-plane. So keep each angle small (rule of thumb under ~3 deg at highway rpm) and equal (within ~1 deg). Gives the per-joint variation and the equal-angle check; the exact max angle for a given rpm comes from the U-joint / driveshaft manufacturer's chart (Spicer/Dana, GMB), and the service manual and the measured pinion / transmission / shaft inclinations govern the setup.
rest.units-of-production-depr: A $50,000 machine, $5,000 salvage, 100,000-unit life used 8,000 units this period depreciates $0.45/unit -> $3,600, book value $46,400. Two catches: an IDLE asset takes zero depreciation that period (time-based methods keep expensing), and the book value can never fall below salvage even past the unit life (run to 110,000 units and it floors at $5,000). A GAAP/book method for hours/miles-driven assets, not tax MACRS. A bookkeeping aid; the accounting policy and tax rules govern.
rest.unit-cost-earthwork: A dozer at $215/hr all-in moving 656 cy/hr costs $0.33/cy, but let production fall to 400 cy/hr on soft ground and it costs $0.54/cy - a 63% jump the rate alone never shows. Low production, not the rate, is what blows up the unit price.
rest.universal-joint-speed: The output ranges between omega cos(beta) and omega/cos(beta), a peak-to-peak swing of 1/cos(beta) - cos(beta) of the input. A joint at 10 degrees on a 1,000 rpm shaft swings the output 985-1,015 rpm (3.1% peak-to-peak); open it to 30 degrees and it explodes to 866-1,155 rpm (29%), which no driveline tolerates. That is why U-joint working angles are held to a few degrees and the two ends of a shaft are angled equally - a second joint phased 90 degrees at an equal angle (double-Cardan) cancels the error. Enter an input torque for the matching torque pulsation (200 lb-ft at 10 degrees swings 197 to 203) and the peak output angular acceleration; the secondary shaking couple and CV joints are separate. A design aid; Machinery Handbook / Shigley and the driveline maker govern.
rest.uv-dose: The delivered ultraviolet dose (intensity x exposure time, mW.s/cm^2 = mJ/cm^2) checked against a validated target (default 40 mJ/cm^2). A short dose points to an aged lamp, a fouled sleeve, or low UV transmittance. USEPA UV Disinfection Guidance; the validated reactor dose and the state primacy agency govern compliance.
rest.uv-required-exposure: From a target dose, solve the operand you are missing - leave intensity blank for the required contact time (dose / intensity), or leave time blank for the required intensity (dose / time). A 40 mJ/cm^2 target at 10 mW/cm^2 needs 4 s of contact; at a fixed 8 s it needs a 5 mW/cm^2 lamp. USEPA UV Disinfection Guidance; the validated reactor dose and the state primacy agency govern compliance.
rest.umbilical-air-supply: Two divers plus a standby at 100 ft, at 1.4 acfm each, need 16.9 scfm -- 5.64 per diver at 4.03 atmospheres -- and a 20 scfm compressor has 3.1 scfm of margin. Take the same spread to 190 ft and the requirement is 28.4 scfm: the compressor no longer meets it, with nothing changed but depth. THE OPERATIONAL LIMIT IS THE NUMBER WORTH HAVING. Working the relation backwards, that compressor supports three divers to 124 ft, and that is worth knowing before the job rather than at the dive station with divers dressed in. THE STANDBY DIVER COUNTS: a spread sized for the divers in the water is undersized. THE RESERVE IS A SEPARATE, REGULATORY CALCULATION. Surface-supplied diving requires an independent reserve breathing supply, sized to bring the diver to the surface from the maximum depth including any required decompression and available without the diver doing anything to switch to it. Ten minutes at 100 ft is 56 cubic feet for one diver against the 85 cubic feet of free gas an 8 cu ft tank at 200 psi can deliver above the 44.5 psig bottom pressure -- so this one covers it, but a volume tank that meets the flow requirement and not the reserve requirement does not comply, and passing one is not passing. A flow and volume calculation on figures the user supplies. The rate per diver is entered because it is set by the applicable regulation and the operation procedures rather than by arithmetic, and the figure that applies depends on the jurisdiction, the mode of diving, and the depth. It does not size an umbilical, evaluate pressure drop along its length, or address the supply pressure the helmet or mask requires at depth, which is a separate and governing check. It does not evaluate air purity, which is its own testing regime, or compressor intake placement, filtration, and carbon monoxide risk. The applicable commercial diving regulations, the operation diving safety manual, and the diving supervisor govern.
rest.ut-thickness-velocity: Thickness is velocity times transit time over two, and the gauge has no way of knowing what material it is sitting on -- so a gauge calibrated on a steel block and used on aluminium reports a number that is precise, repeatable, documented, and wrong by about 7 percent. THE ERROR IS A PERCENTAGE, AND IT SCALES WITH THE WALL. That is worth stating plainly because it is easy to carry an absolute figure across from one thickness to another: 7 percent of a 5 inch section is about three hundred forty thousandths and 7 percent of a half-inch wall is thirty-four, and both are serious for different reasons. The figure that matters is the one computed at the wall actually being inspected. THE TWO DIRECTIONS ARE NOT EQUALLY DANGEROUS. A gauge reading LOW retires equipment early, which costs money. A gauge reading HIGH leaves a wall in service that is already below its retirement limit, and the report says it passed. Against a stated limit this reports the thinnest wall that still reads acceptable, because that gap is the exposure the calibration error creates and it is invisible in the reading itself. Coating is the other silent overread. Sound crosses paint at roughly a third of steel's velocity, so in single-echo mode a coated wall reads thick by considerably more than the coating's own thickness -- again in the unsafe direction. Echo-to-echo mode times between two back-wall echoes and ignores everything in front of them, which is why it is the mode for any coated corrosion survey, and why a survey done in the wrong mode on a painted tank is not conservative. The rule that follows from all of it: CALIBRATE ON A KNOWN THICKNESS OF THE ACTUAL MATERIAL, and re-calibrate when the material changes. A velocity table is a starting point, not a calibration, because velocity varies with alloy, temperature and grain structure. This is the velocity relation and its consequences. It does not select a transducer, frequency or couplant, address surface preparation, curvature, or high-temperature measurement (velocity falls with temperature, and a hot survey needs its own correction), interpret A-scans, distinguish general wall loss from pitting (a gauge finds the thickness under the probe and a pit between readings is missed entirely), evaluate laminations or inclusions, or determine a retirement limit. API 570, API 653 or the applicable inspection code, the equipment's fitness-for-service assessment, and the certified inspector govern.
rest.usr-vertical-shore-capacity: A 3-post shore of Douglas Fir 4x4s at 10 ft has an L/D of 34.3, an allowable stress of 408 psi, and 5,002 lb per post -- the guide's 5,000 -- so 15,006 lb of capacity against a 12,000 lb load, a ratio of 0.80. In Hem-Fir the ratio rises to 0.94. Cut to 6 ft, the same post is below the 20.9 crossover, the cap governs, and it carries 13,475 lb, 2.7 times as much. The L/D of 25 is a warning limit, not a strength limit: past it a post can buckle before its ends crush and creak, and the calculator flags it -- including at the guide's own headline 4x4 in an 8 ft shore, which sits at 27.4. Beyond 50 the post is refused. Lateral bracing is reported at 2% of the vertical capacity and 10% where aftershocks are expected. It overlaps the Wood Column Capacity (Slenderness) calculator, which applies the NDS method to one member; this is the distinct US&R field procedure. It does not design headers, check bearing across the grain, cover laced posts or proprietary struts, or evaluate the ground under the sole. The US&R guides, the US&R Structures Specialist, and the incident's structural engineer govern.
rest.usr-crib-capacity: The US&R Shoring Operations Guide writes it L = A x N x P: the area of one crossing, times the crossings per layer (4 for a 2x2 layup, 9 for 3x3), times 500 psi across the grain for No. 1 and better Douglas Fir, with the same 0.85 and 0.75 species factors as vertical shores. A 3x3 crib of 6x6 Spruce-Pine-Fir is 30.25 x 9 x 500 = 136,125 lb, or 115,706 lb after the species factor -- the guide rounds the Douglas Fir figure to 135,000. A 2x2 of 4x4 Douglas Fir is 24,500 lb against the guide's 24,000. The crushing failure is slow and audible, which is why cribbing is trusted. Height is a stability limit that tightens as the crib loses contact: three times the narrowest width with every point bearing, two for lift-and-crib work, one and a half on two of four corners, one on a single corner, and a practical ceiling of about 4 ft for 4x4 and 6 ft for 6x6 cribbing. A 4 ft wide 6x6 crib is limited to 6 ft by the practical ceiling, not the 12 ft ratio; on one bearing corner it falls to 4 ft, and a crib that must be taller is widened, not stacked. The 2006 Field Operations Guide lists 625 psi rather than 500, so the stress is an input with the 2021 value as the default. It does not check the surface under the crib, wedges and shims, lateral stability, or plastic cribbing. The US&R guides, the US&R Structures Specialist, and the incident's structural engineer govern.
rest.usr-raker-shore: The guides design each raker for about 10% of the weight of the wall and roof in its tributary width, 2% where no aftershock is expected. A 12 in unreinforced masonry wall at 125 psf, 14 ft tall, with rakers at 8 ft centers and an 8 by 10 ft roof area at 15 psf, weighs 15,200 lb per raker, for a design force of 1,520 lb. Inserted at 12 ft and set at 45 degrees, the raker is 203.6 in long (the field rule of 17 in per foot gives 204), stands 12 ft out from the wall, and carries 2,150 lb along its length with a 1,520 lb upward kick at the wall plate. At 60 degrees it is 166.3 in long (rule 168), its base shrinks to 7 ft, but the axial force rises to 3,040 lb and the kick to 2,633 lb. That kick is the part most often missed: a wall plate that is only nailed can be pushed up the wall. The two guide editions rate rakers differently and both are shown -- the 2021 Shoring Operations Guide at 4,000 lb of horizontal force per raker (8,000 lb for a braced pair), the 2006 Field Operations Guide at 2,500 lb. The collapse zone, 1.25 to 1.5 times the wall height, reaches 21 ft here, beyond the 45 degree base, so the crew works inside it. It does not design the plate, sole, cleats, bracing, or ground restraint, or check the wall between rakers. The US&R guides, the US&R Structures Specialist, and the incident's structural engineer govern.
